description: Justice in Surah An-Nisa, the sin of shirk, and the nature and role of Shari'ah law in Muslim life.
content_html:
Justice in Surah An-Nisa (Surah 4:105–135)

Surah An-Nisa (Surah 4, “The Women”) is one of the longest chapters in the Qur’an and covers a wide range of legal and social teachings. Verses 105–135 focus particularly on justice. The Qur’an’s vision of justice is comprehensive — it covers legal fairness in courts, economic fairness, treatment of the poor, and the rights of women, orphans and prisoners.

In Surah 4:135, Allah commands: “O you who believe! Stand out firmly for justice, as witnesses to Allah, even if it be against yourselves, your parents, or your relatives, or whether it be against the rich or the poor.” This is a demanding standard — justice must be impartial even when it is personally costly. A Muslim is expected to testify truthfully even against their own family.

The Qur’an also connects justice to the character of Allah. Because Allah is Just (Al-‘Adl, one of the 99 names), human beings as his khalifah on earth are required to mirror that justice in their institutions and relationships. In Shi’a Islam, Adl (divine justice) is one of the Five Roots of faith, making it even more central to that tradition’s theology.

The Hadith traditions also illustrate justice in practice. The Prophet Muhammad’s recorded sayings and actions (Hadith) show him returning stolen goods, insisting that even a powerful person should be punished for wrongdoing, and declaring that “whoever does not show mercy will not be shown mercy.” These traditions show justice as lived, practical and applied, not merely theological.

Key Fact

Surah 4:135 commands Muslims to “stand out firmly for justice… even if it be against yourselves, your parents, or your relatives.” This makes justice a binding obligation that overrides personal loyalty. It connects to the Islamic concept of Adl (divine justice) — because Allah is Just, Muslims must be just even at personal cost.

Shirk: The Greatest Sin

Shirk means to ascribe partners to Allah — to associate anything or anyone with his divine nature. It is the opposite of Tawhid (the oneness of Allah) and is considered the gravest sin in Islam. The Qur’an states repeatedly that Allah may forgive any sin except shirk for those who die without repenting.

Shirk takes several forms. The most obvious is idol worship — worshipping statues or images as gods. Surah 7:148–150 recounts the story of the Israelites who made and worshipped a golden calf while Moses was receiving the Torah on Sinai. Moses returned to find the people in this act of shirk and was furious. The story is a vivid illustration of how easily human beings fall into substituting a visible, created thing for the invisible, eternal God.

More subtle forms of shirk include: placing ultimate trust or fear in human beings or institutions rather than Allah; following desires (the “lower self”) as if they were divine commands; and giving to human relationships the devotion that belongs only to Allah. Muslim scholars have also identified “hidden shirk” — performing religious acts for human approval rather than sincerely for Allah.

For Muslims today, the condemnation of shirk shapes their approach to other religions. Some Muslim scholars argue that Christian Trinitarian theology — which speaks of God as Father, Son and Holy Spirit — approaches shirk by attributing a partner (Jesus) to Allah. Most Muslims, however, engage respectfully with Christians and Jews as “People of the Book,” recognising the partial truth in their scriptures while maintaining the Islamic insistence on strict divine unity.

The story of the golden calf in Surah 7:148–150 parallels the account in Exodus 32 but with some differences. In the Qur’anic version, the Israelites made the calf in Moses’s absence and worshipped it; they “could not see that it could not speak to them or guide them any way.” Moses returned, cast down the calf and rebuked his brother Aaron for allowing it. The idols’ inability to speak, guide or help their worshippers is a recurring Qur’anic argument against idolatry: only Allah can respond, guide and provide.

The story teaches that shirk is a moral as well as a theological failure — it involves a refusal to reason carefully about what is worthy of worship. The Qur’an repeatedly challenges idol-worshippers to explain how a created thing can have divine attributes. Ibrahim’s famous destruction of his people’s idols (discussed in a later lesson) makes the same point with dramatic action.

Shari’ah Law

Shari’ah means “path” or “way” in Arabic — the path that Allah has revealed for human beings to follow. It is not simply a legal code but a comprehensive guide to how a Muslim should live in relationship with Allah, with other people, and with the natural world. Shari’ah covers worship (ibadat), relationships and family (muamalat), criminal law (uqubat), and social ethics.

Surah 4:59–60 is one of the foundational Qur’anic verses for Shari’ah: “O you who believe! Obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you. And if you disagree about anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger.” This verse establishes the hierarchy of Islamic legal authority: first the Qur’an (Allah), then the Sunnah (the Prophet’s practice and sayings), then the rulings of qualified scholars.

Surah 33:21–36 reinforces the idea that the Prophet Muhammad is the model for the Muslim community. Verse 21 states: “Certainly you have in the Messenger of Allah an excellent example.” This is the Qur’anic basis for the Sunnah as a source of Islamic law alongside the Qur’an — if you want to know how to live, look at how the Prophet lived.

From an atheist or Humanist perspective, following a religious legal code such as Shari’ah is problematic for several reasons. First, they would argue that laws should derive from democratic consent and human reason, not from texts claimed to be divine revelation. Second, they might point to specific rulings in classical Shari’ah (on gender equality, religious freedom, or punishments) that appear in tension with modern human rights standards. Third, they would question the principle that God’s command is a sufficient basis for law without independent moral justification.

Muslims respond in a number of ways. Many distinguish between the unchanging core of Shari’ah (the principles of justice, compassion and care for the vulnerable) and the specific rulings that were developed in a historical context and can be reinterpreted. Modern Muslim scholars such as Tariq Ramadan argue that Shari’ah is best understood as an ethical framework rather than a rigid legal code. Muslims in democratic societies typically observe the personal dimensions of Shari’ah (prayer, fasting, halal food) while living under civil law.

Key Fact

Shari’ah means “path” — the comprehensive guide to Muslim life. Its sources are the Qur’an and the Sunnah (the Prophet’s practice). Surah 4:59 establishes the hierarchy: “Obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those in authority.” Shari’ah covers worship, family, ethics and legal matters, and is understood differently by different Muslim communities around the world.
exam_tip_html: For 5-mark questions on Shari’ah, name a surah reference: “In Surah 4:59, Allah commands obedience to himself, the Messenger and those in authority…” earns the source mark. For questions on shirk, you can use Surah 7:148–150 (the golden calf) as your source. For 12-mark Discuss questions on Shari’ah being ‘unnecessary in modern society,’ develop the Humanist/atheist argument fully (democratic consent, human rights tensions) before presenting the Muslim response — the most common failure is treating the opposing view as a single dismissive sentence. SPaG: spell ‘Shari’ah’ with the apostrophe and the ‘h’ at the end; spell ‘shirk’ in lower case (it is a common noun, not a proper name). Use ‘Adl’ when referring to divine justice in Shi’a Islam.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Surah An-Nisa (4:105–135) commands justice even against oneself and one’s own family; Allah’s justice (Adl) is a Shi’a root of faith and a model for all Muslims in their social and legal relationships.
  • Shirk (associating partners with Allah) is the gravest sin in Islam — Surah 7:148–150 illustrates it through the golden calf; it is the opposite of Tawhid and shapes Muslim approaches to worship and other religions.
  • Shari’ah (the ‘path’) is the comprehensive Islamic guide to life derived from the Qur’an and Sunnah (Surah 4:59); it covers worship, ethics and law, and is understood diversely by different Muslim communities today.

practice_questions.text: Outline three things that the Qur'an teaches about justice in Surah An-Nisa.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per discrete point:
• Surah 4:135 commands Muslims to stand firmly for justice even against themselves, their parents or their relatives.
• Justice must be impartial — it should not favour the rich over the poor or the powerful over the weak.
• Justice is grounded in Allah's own character as Al-'Adl (the Just) — because Allah is just, humans are required to be just as his stewards on earth.

practice_questions.text: Describe what shirk means and why it is considered so serious in Islam.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per point:
• Shirk means associating partners with Allah — giving to any created thing the worship or ultimate loyalty that belongs to Allah alone.
• It is the opposite of Tawhid (the oneness of Allah) and is considered the one sin that cannot be forgiven if persisted in until death.
• The Qur'an condemns idolatry as a form of shirk — Surah 7:148-150 illustrates this with the golden calf story.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Shari'ah law is important for Muslims today.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per point:
• Shari'ah provides a comprehensive guide to worship and personal conduct — daily prayer, fasting, halal food laws and zakah are all part of Shari'ah, giving Muslim life a coherent, God-centred structure that goes beyond merely following human custom.
• Shari'ah provides a framework for justice and ethics — its principles of fairness, care for the vulnerable and prohibition of exploitation are applied in Muslim communities around the world, whether in full legal systems or in personal ethical choices.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two ways in which the teaching about shirk shapes how Muslims live today.
In your answer, refer to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per point plus one for named source:
• Shirk shapes Muslim worship: because ascribing partners to Allah is forbidden, all prayer and devotion must be directed to Allah alone — no image, statue or mediating figure can be the object of worship. This is why mosques are adorned with geometric patterns and calligraphy rather than images of Allah or the prophets.
• Shirk shapes Muslim responses to other religions: Islam's insistence on Tawhid means Muslims cannot accept Trinitarian Christianity or Hindu polytheism as fully valid, though they recognise the People of the Book (Jews and Christians) as having received earlier revelation from Allah.
The fifth mark requires citing Surah 7:148-150 (golden calf) or another shirk-related passage as the named source.

practice_questions.text:
'Following Shari'ah law is unnecessary for Muslims living in modern Britain.'
Discuss this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; justified conclusion.
Secure (7-9): Both sides present; at least one source.
Developing (4-6): One side stronger; few sources.
Emerging (1-3): Minimal.

In support (of the statement): Humanists argue that ethics should be based on human reason and democratic consent, not divine commands. Some Shari'ah rulings developed in 7th-century Arabia may not be appropriate for 21st-century Britain. Muslims in Britain live under civil law, which already provides frameworks for justice and rights. Following Shari'ah in all details would create two parallel legal systems.
Against: The Qur'an commands obedience to Allah and the Messenger (Surah 4:59) — for committed Muslims, Shari'ah is not optional but an expression of submission to Allah. Even in Britain, Muslims observe many aspects of Shari'ah (prayer times, halal food, fasting, family law in some cases). Many Muslim scholars argue Shari'ah's principles of justice, compassion and care for the vulnerable are entirely compatible with modern life. The Sunnah (Surah 33:21-36) provides the model for how Shari'ah is lived — adaptable to context while rooted in divine guidance.

practice_questions.text: Outline three ways in which the golden calf story in Surah 7:148-150 illustrates the problem of shirk.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per discrete point:
• The Israelites made and worshipped a physical image in Moses's absence — this substituted a visible, created thing for the invisible, eternal God.
• The calf could not speak, guide or help its worshippers — this shows the Qur'an's argument that idols are powerless compared to Allah.
• Moses's anger on his return demonstrates how seriously shirk is treated — it is a betrayal of the covenant relationship with Allah.

glossary_terms.definition: Surah 4 — 'The Women'; one of the longest surahs, dealing with family law, justice, and the treatment of those in society.
'Adl in Arabic — the fair, impartial treatment of people according to what they deserve; a core divine attribute and human obligation in Islam.
Divine justice — one of the Five Roots of Usul ad-Din in Shi'a Islam; the belief that Allah is perfectly just and that every human action will be judged fairly.
The recorded sayings, actions and approvals of the Prophet Muhammad; the second source of Islamic law and ethics after the Qur'an.
The sin of ascribing partners to Allah, or associating anything with God; considered the gravest sin in Islam, which alone cannot be forgiven if persisted in until death.
The comprehensive religious law of Islam, derived from the Qur'an and Sunnah; it covers all areas of life from worship to ethics to legal matters.
